name: Phantacite
description: Phantacite is a next-generation psychedelic that doesn't produce random hallucinations — it interfaces directly with the user's BCI to generate structured, navigable hallucinatory environments built from the user's own neural aesthetic vocabulary. The trip feels designed rather than chaotic: beautiful, meaningful, and deeply personal. Helix sells curated 'experience architectures' as optional paid DLC that can shape the hallucination's broad strokes while leaving the fine detail to the user's unconscious.
effects: Structured, navigable hallucinations built from personal neural aesthetic patterns
Profound sense of meaning and self-discovery
Visual and auditory hallucinations with internal logical consistency
Deep introspective insights that feel permanently true
side_effects: Insights that feel profound during the trip and nonsensical afterward — and occasionally the reverse
BCI feedback artifacts lasting 24 hours post-use
Rare: hallucination architecture that the user cannot distinguish from memory after the fact
Anxiety and paranoia if the trip turns negative
Users with certain BCI models experience uncontrolled interface activity during the peak
street_price: Φ 350 per dose (base); Φ 600+ with premium Helix experience architectures
cultural_context: Phantacite is GLMZ's prestige psychedelic — it's what people mean when they talk about 'doing serious work on yourself.' Tier 3 and 4 users approach Phantacite trips with intention, preparation, and integration journals. There's a robust guide community — people who sit with trippers and help them navigate the architecture. Helix's paid experience architectures are controversial: critics argue that selling shaped trips makes the drug a luxury consumption product rather than a genuine exploration tool, and that the architectures subtly push users toward emotional conclusions favorable to Helix's brand positioning.
story_hooks: A Helix experience architecture called 'Reconciliation' is producing identical emotional breakthroughs in unrelated users — everyone who uses it comes out convinced they need to forgive a specific authority figure in their life, and a journalist thinks the architecture is not neutral

A user's Phantacite trip generated a hallucination that contained accurate information they had no conscious access to — architectural details of a location they'd never visited, technical specifications for a system they didn't know existed — and they can't explain it

A street version of Phantacite is circulating without BCI interface capability, forcing the hallucinations to run purely chemically — the trips are reportedly terrifying and completely unstructured, and several users have emerged from them genuinely changed in ways that worry the people who love them
